⌂ BERKELEY DECISION PROJECT
Better questions. Better evidence. Better choices.

The waterfront

Happily Never After: A Ferry Tale

Berkeley is being asked to remake an irreplaceable stretch of waterfront for a ferry whose future is far from assured.

The pier is built to last fifty years. WETA’s operating funds run out after 2034.

What happens if the ferry succeeds? What happens if it doesn’t?

  1. ◆ The stakes
  2. I Paying to build it
  3. II Finding the riders

  5. IV Paying to run it

  7. VI Displacing its users

  9. ◆ A cautionary tale

The stakes · The promise

The promise: a better waterfront and a cleaner way across the Bay.

  • A rebuilt public pier and more ways to enjoy the waterfront.
  • Visitors who arrive by transit, bike and on foot.
  • A zero-emission ferry to San Francisco, with fares and travel times that compete with BART and driving.
  • Fewer people driving alone across the Bay, and less traffic and pollution.
  • A ferry that fits alongside the sailing, swimming and fishing already here.
  • A way across the Bay when an emergency closes the bridges, BART or the roads.

But…

The stakes · If everything goes right

Even the best case depends on long odds.

How secure is each line?
  • Certain Follows from the design or a binding rule
  • Planned Written into a City or WETA plan that can still change
  • Forecast Holds only if projections come true
  • Unfunded Designed and costed; no money identified
  • No plan No way to deliver it has been named
  • 🧙 Magical Thinking Not impossible in principle: the plan depends on something no one has budgeted, built or found
  • UnfundedThe pier reopens at 1,080 feet, with a plaza and a Bay Trail link.Designed and estimated at $103.6 million, but “construction funding has not been identified.”
  • 🧙Magical ThinkingTwo electric boats run weekday service to San Francisco.No 250-passenger electric ferry exists or is on order: WETA builds them in 150- and 400-passenger sizes, and who pays for the boats “will be determined at a future date.”
  • ForecastRiders meet WETA’s forecast: 915 weekday boardings at opening, 1,160 riders at full service. The forecast counts riders from anywhere: a driver from Stockton counts the same as a resident of West Berkeley. That works for WETA. It makes no sense for Berkeley to pay for.WETA has a forecast; the City’s parking plan says year one is “unlikely to reach WETA’s projected levels.”
  • 🧙Magical ThinkingAbout 1,000 riders a day are served with about 250 parking spaces.The spaces do not exist: the City’s parking plan counts 314 to 347 cars a weekday in the first year against 265 all-day stalls, and sends the rest to Marina Blvd and University Ave.
  • ForecastBy year ten, fares cover 52% of the cost of the San Francisco route. The rider pays $6.74 a trip and the public $6.35, $4.3 million in 2035.Holds only if riders reach 100% of forecast and fares rise every year for a decade.
  • No planRegional money fills the gap, and Berkeley pays nothing toward operations.No source is named. WETA’s money is funded through FY2034, it requires ten years, and its Board expects Berkeley to pay half.
  • PlannedBerkeley still subsidizes the region. WETA’s policy makes the City own, maintain and fund the terminal’s parking and landside assets, for riders the plan draws from Albany, Emeryville and beyond.WETA’s access policy, presented for Board adoption in November 2024, assigns landside ownership, maintenance and funding to the City; the business plan’s market includes Albany and Emeryville.
  • CertainThe waterfront gains 1,127 new car trips a day.The Draft EIR’s count.
  • PlannedThe ferry sits in a park the Bay Plan protects: a terminal may not “interfere with current or future park and recreational uses,” and park parking “should not be usurped by ferry patrons.” To make room for commuters, the City’s parking plan puts the recreation lots on four-hour limits for anyone who arrives after 6 a.m.Written into the City’s draft parking plan, to be adjusted after service begins.
  • 🧙Magical ThinkingThe emergency backup runs on the power grid. The dock batteries cover “short-term power disruptions”; for a real outage, WETA “envisions” bringing in a power barge. The Draft EIR does not analyze emergency operations at all.The power barge WETA “envisions” is not budgeted and does not exist: the City’s $103.6 million estimate carries no barge, and the Draft EIR names none. A disaster that closes the bridge and BART can take down the grid too; the dock batteries cover only “short-term power disruptions.”

Every one of these conditions must hold at once for the best case to arrive, and even then the waterfront bears the cost.

The stakes · If the uncertainties break the wrong way

Berkeley could be left paying for a ferry that no longer runs.

  • Construction money does not arrive for a $103.6 million terminal, before boats, and the project stops between phases.Mitigation: Build in phases as money arrives. Stretching the money is how a project stalls between phases.
  • Berkeley borrows its share, at least $30 million. No source has been identified, and the Measure U bond list carries no ferry project.Mitigation: none identified
  • Riders come slowly, as the City’s parking plan expects in year one. Richmond, with as many riders, covers 11 to 12 percent of its cost from fares.Mitigation: Adjust the parking rules; WETA marketing. Both assume parking and awareness are what keep riders away, and the plans never test that assumption.
  • The boats stay diesel: the business plan priced diesel, and WETA’s electric transition “hinges on new funds.”Mitigation: none identified
  • WETA’s operating money runs out after FY2034, or after FY2031 without electrification savings: three to six years into the ten a new route requires.Mitigation: Cut service, and “seek new non-RM3 funding sources”: money someone else decides to give, which Berkeley cannot guarantee.
  • WETA uses the levers its plan names for an underperforming route: move its funding, cut its service.Mitigation: none identified
  • WETA expects Berkeley to pay half the annual operating subsidy—at least $4.5 million a year. Berkeley says it isn’t obligated to pay. But if regional funding runs short, the City could face a choice: subsidize a ferry serving riders from across the East Bay, or risk losing the service altogether.Mitigation: none identified
  • Berkeley keeps a pier built to last fifty years, the breakwater, the dredged channel and the rebuilt lots, with a Marina Fund the City Manager called “on the brink of insolvency” in 2021.Mitigation: none identified

For most of these risks, the plans name no mitigation. Where they do, the fix stalls the project, bets on an untested assumption, or waits on someone else’s money.

The stakes · If it succeeds beyond the forecast

Even success leaves Berkeley with more cars and a distressed marina.

  • Ridership beats the forecast, the farebox improves, and WETA has a route that justifies itself.
  • More riders bring more cars. The business plan expects 68% to arrive by car, and at the forecast ridership demand already outruns the 265 all-day stalls.
  • The four-hour limits and paid parking on the recreation lots tighten as demand grows: the plan’s adjustments include “changes to parking fees, permit types and restrictions.”
  • Berkeley collects parking revenue, which the City counts on to “offset the structural deficit in the Marina Fund.”
  • The Marina gains little else. The City’s consultant found ferry service “will likely generate very modest direct revenues to the Marina Fund.” Its promise that the ferry will draw a new hotel is magical thinking: one sentence, with no hotel operator or developer named, and the consultant’s hotel study mentions the ferry only as a source of restaurant customers. At Jack London Square, a ferry with more than 2,000 daily boardings sits beside ground-floor retail more than half vacant, and the Waterfront Hotel has closed.
  • The Marina stays distressed: $153 million in unfunded waterfront needs, and a Marina Fund the City Manager called “on the brink of insolvency,” against ferry revenue the City’s consultant calls very modest.
  • More riders from El Cerrito and beyond use a terminal whose parking and landside costs fall on Berkeley.
  • University Avenue carries more than the 1,127 new daily car trips the Draft EIR counts at the forecast.

WETA’s numbers improve with success. Berkeley’s costs grow with it, and the park gets worse to visit.

The stakes · Either way

The waterfront pays first, either way.

  • About 40 trees and the berm that shelters the South Cove come out.
  • The Seawall Lot is torn up and rebuilt: pavement, parking islands, trees and the berm all removed.
  • Up to 400,000 cubic yards of dredging, and a channel to keep open after.
  • Construction noise the Draft EIR calls significant and unavoidable, with up to 50 nights of pile driving.

All of this arrives with construction, before the first rider, whatever ridership turns out to be.

The voyage · I · Paying to build it

No one has found the money to build it

The City’s estimate for the terminal is $103.6 million, before a single boat. In the City’s words: “Construction funding has not been identified.”

The plan
Build in phases, “based on funding sources and timing.”
Reality check
With the boats and the second berth, the full project runs past $200 million, and Berkeley’s share is at least $30 million.
Why it matters

The estimate covers demolition, the pier, the breakwater, the terminal, $26 million of dredging, the parking lot, the trail and the plaza. It leaves out the vessels, which WETA’s business plan prices at about $16 million each, and it leaves open who pays for what: the plan says the shares “will be determined at a future date.”

The City’s answer to the missing money is to build in phases as funding arrives. A phased project approved without its funding can stop between phases, with the waterfront already rebuilt around a ferry that has not arrived.

Sources and figures
ObligationFund construction before committing the waterfront to it.
ObstacleNo construction source has been named. Dredging alone is $26 million of the estimate; the boats are not in it at all.
The planBuild in phases, “based on funding sources and timing.”
Reality checkWith the boats and the second berth, the full project runs past $200 million, and Berkeley’s share is at least $30 million.
Who bears itBerkeley, if the project stops part-built
Can it be undone?Each completed phase is permanent.

The voyage · II · Finding the riders

Two-thirds of the riders are expected to drive to it

WETA’s business plan has 68% of passengers reaching the terminal by car and 5% by transit. The terminal sits about a mile from where Berkeley’s population begins.

The plan
Paid parking, a transportation demand program, a bus stop and a cycle track.
Reality check
The City’s parking plan says first-year ridership is “unlikely to reach WETA’s projected levels immediately.” The business plan never estimates how many riders would come from BART.
Why it matters

The forecast is 915 weekday boardings at opening, growing to 1,160 riders at full service. Those riders have to come from somewhere. WETA’s plan says walking to the terminal “will be impractical for many trips,” so most will drive to the Marina and park.

Driving to the ferry is still driving. BART and AC Transit run through the neighborhoods where people live; the ferry sits a mile past the freeway, at the end of a road. A commuter who leaves the train or the bus for the ferry trades transit from near home for a drive to the Marina. WETA’s survey shows how common that rider is, and the business plan never counts them.

Sources and figures
ObligationEnough riders to meet the forecast, and riders who would otherwise drive across the Bay.
ObstacleA remote site, and a regional alternative: in WETA’s 2024 survey, 45% of ferry riders systemwide named BART or other rail as their alternative. On the Richmond route in 2025, it was 65%.
The planPaid parking, a transportation demand program, a bus stop and a cycle track.
Reality checkThe City’s parking plan says first-year ridership is “unlikely to reach WETA’s projected levels immediately.” The business plan never estimates how many riders would come from BART.
Who bears itThe climate case; the farebox; waterfront parking
Can it be undone?n/a

The voyage · III · Getting the boats

Sold as zero-emission. Priced as diesel.

The business plan that sets the fares and the subsidy models two 250-passenger diesel boats. No electric boat is on order for the Berkeley route.

The plan
The Draft EIR assumes electric boats and a battery charging float that has not yet been designed.
Reality check
WETA’s zero-emission transition “hinges on new funds becoming available.” Only a binding condition of approval would make electric boats more than a promise.
Why it matters

Two documents describe two different ferries. The environmental review assumes electric boats, so the emissions come out low. The business plan runs the numbers on diesel, because “reliable cost information for electric zero-emission vessels is limited.”

Electric boats should cost less to run. They cost far more to buy: priced from WETA’s fleet and its electric order, an electric seat costs roughly twice a diesel one and moves fewer trips a day. No 250-passenger electric boat exists, and who pays for the boats “will be determined at a future date.” A fleet promise carries the weight of a condition only when someone can enforce it.

Sources and figures
ObligationZero-emission service, as WETA’s letter to residents promises.
ObstacleWETA builds electric ferries in 150- and 400-passenger sizes. An electric seat costs 1.7 to 2.2 times a diesel one, at two-thirds the speed.
The planThe Draft EIR assumes electric boats and a battery charging float that has not yet been designed.
Reality checkWETA’s zero-emission transition “hinges on new funds becoming available.” Only a binding condition of approval would make electric boats more than a promise.
Who bears itBerkeley’s climate case; residents near the terminal
Can it be undone?A future fleet can change; an approval without a condition cannot add one.

The voyage · IV · Paying to run it

There is no plan to pay to run the boats

WETA requires a dedicated funding source for at least ten years of operations on any new route. Berkeley’s has none: WETA’s operating money is fully funded through FY2034, and the Berkeley route starts in FY2029, at $5.9 million a year.

The plan
Spend reserves, which WETA projects will last through FY2034, and “seek new non-RM3 funding sources.” WETA’s business plan suggests a Berkeley hotel-tax surcharge.
Reality check
WETA’s Board expects Berkeley to pay half the annual subsidy: at least $4.5 million a year, for a route that needs $9 to $12 million. Berkeley would be paying for a regional service: a driver from El Cerrito rides on the same subsidy.
Why it matters

The City’s FAQ says Berkeley is not required to subsidize the ferry, and gives the reason: WETA’s expansion policy “requires a dedicated funding source for at least ten years of operations for any new routes.” WETA’s October 2024 plan funds its whole system, Berkeley included, through FY2034, and through FY2031 if electrification savings do not arrive. From FY2026 on it balances the budget by spending reserves.

Richmond is the closest comparison: about as many weekday riders as Berkeley is projected to carry, through a much simpler terminal to maintain. WETA cut Richmond’s fare from $7 to $4.50 in its pandemic recovery program; it is now $4.70. The riders came with the low fare, and the subsidy came with the riders. WETA’s corrective actions for an underperforming route include moving its funding to other routes, and its plan for stretching the money includes service cuts.

The money comes mostly from bridge tolls. In WETA’s FY2029 plan, Regional Measure 1, 2 and 3 toll funds are 60% of operating revenue, fares 25%, and the rest is state transit assistance and local taxes. Richmond’s route has a Contra Costa County sales tax behind it, Measure J, $4.4 million that year. Berkeley’s route has no local source: the City says it is not required to pay, and the business plan proposes a Berkeley hotel-tax surcharge.

The riders will not all be Berkeley residents. WETA’s business plan draws its market from Albany, Berkeley and Emeryville together, and On Richmond’s route, WETA’s 2025 survey found only 55% of San Francisco–bound riders starting their trip in Richmond, and 8% of homebound riders headed on to El Cerrito. The City’s parking plan simply assumes every boarding originates in Berkeley. A Berkeley subsidy at a terminal reached by car is a Berkeley payment for a regional benefit.

WETA’s RM3 farebox standard is relative: a ferry route’s requirement is capped at what comparable express buses must meet, or the route can instead show farebox growth year over year. The state goal is 40%.

Sources and figures
ObligationA dedicated operating source for at least ten years, which WETA’s expansion policy requires of any new route.
ObstacleThe toll money is already spoken for; WETA is drawing down reserves to balance its budget.
The planSpend reserves, which WETA projects will last through FY2034, and “seek new non-RM3 funding sources.” WETA’s business plan suggests a Berkeley hotel-tax surcharge.
Reality checkWETA’s Board expects Berkeley to pay half the annual subsidy: at least $4.5 million a year, for a route that needs $9 to $12 million. Berkeley would be paying for a regional service: a driver from El Cerrito rides on the same subsidy.
Who bears itBerkeley, at least $4.5 million a year; riders, if service is cut
Can it be undone?The subsidy can stop; the service stops with it.

The voyage · V · Changing the waterfront

Forty trees and the South Cove’s windbreak come out

The Draft EIR removes about 40 trees and the Seawall Drive berm to rebuild the parking lot and make room for the plaza and trail.

The plan
Plant 50 to 70 new 24-inch-box trees across the plaza, parking lot and medians.
Reality check
Replanting replaces landscaping. The Draft EIR lists the berm as vegetation to remove and does not assess the wind it blocks, though scoping comments asked for wind analysis.
Why it matters

The trees and the berm protect the South Cove, where sailing students start. The project treats them as landscaping. Its answer is new trees in 24-inch boxes, which take years to grow, and no new berm.

This change happens on the first day of construction. It does not depend on a single rider showing up.

The Draft EIR says most of the trees to be removed are in poor health.

Sources and figures
ObligationKeep the South Cove sheltered enough for beginners to learn to sail.
ObstacleThe trees and berm along Seawall Drive are part of what blocks the wind there.
The planPlant 50 to 70 new 24-inch-box trees across the plaza, parking lot and medians.
Reality checkReplanting replaces landscaping. The Draft EIR lists the berm as vegetation to remove and does not assess the wind it blocks, though scoping comments asked for wind analysis.
Who bears itSailing students and small-boat programs in the South Cove
Can it be undone?Not reversible on any useful timescale.

The voyage · V · Changing the waterfront

Land filled in 1967 for a park, a beach and their parking becomes a commuter lot

BCDC let Berkeley fill the Bay at Seawall Drive in 1966 and 1967 for a restaurant, a public beach, a park, a plaza, a walkway and the parking that serves them, to “permanently establish public access and recreational use for a sizable part of the Berkeley shoreline.”

The plan
Paid all-day stalls open to any visitor, ferry riders included, under a BCDC paid-parking permit not yet granted.
Reality check
The 1966 permit has never been amended. Berkeley told BCDC the lot “would be used primarily for patrons of the restaurant, park and beach.” A weekday commuter lot is a different use, and BCDC voted in August 2026 to hear the paid-parking application as a major permit.
Why it matters

The land the ferry parking would occupy is not original shoreline. It is Bay fill, approved by the Bay Conservation and Development Commission on the City’s promise of a public waterfront: Permit No. 1966.028.00 for “a marina restaurant, public beach, park area, automobile parking, and a relocated and expanded University of California sailing facility,” and Permit No. 1967.002.00 for a plaza, parking and a walkway along Seawall Drive to the fishing pier.

The Commission exists to stop Bay fill. It allowed this fill because the use was recreation. Turning that parking into a weekday lot for commuters changes the bargain the fill was granted on.

Sources and figures
ObligationKeep the filled land for the public recreation it was filled for.
ObstacleThe parking plan turns 200 stalls of the Seawall Lot into paid all-day parking on weekdays, sized for ferry commuters.
The planPaid all-day stalls open to any visitor, ferry riders included, under a BCDC paid-parking permit not yet granted.
Reality checkThe 1966 permit has never been amended. Berkeley told BCDC the lot “would be used primarily for patrons of the restaurant, park and beach.” A weekday commuter lot is a different use, and BCDC voted in August 2026 to hear the paid-parking application as a major permit.
Who bears itRecreational visitors
Can it be undone?The parking rules can change; a terminal built around commuter parking makes them hard to change back.

The voyage · VI · Displacing its users

Four-hour limits at the South Cove for anyone who arrives after 6 a.m.

The City’s draft parking plan puts every lot near the landing on permits or a four-hour limit, a limit that “does not accommodate ferry commuters.” A full day on the water means arriving before 6 a.m. to prepay at South Cove West.

The plan
Send all-day parkers to 265 paid stalls, or to free parking on Marina Blvd and University Ave.
Reality check
Commuters are projected to fill the paid stalls, and the free all-day parking is up to a third of a mile from the launches. The Draft EIR heard that ferry parking would crowd out swimmers, windsurfers, kayakers and anglers, and analyzed it as car noise.
Why it matters

The lots nearest the landing, from the South Cove lots to O Lot and Seawall Drive, serve the sailing docks and Shorebird Beach, where windsurfers, wingers, swimmers, paddlers and kayakers put in. To keep commuters out of them, the plan caps them at four hours from 9 to 5. That cap applies to everyone who arrives after 6 a.m.; only South Cove West sells prepaid full-day parking, and only before then, because the first ferry leaves at 6:30.

A visitor who needs the day moves to paid all-day stalls or to free parking that, by the Boardsailing Association’s measure, sits up to a third of a mile from the launches. The Association says that distance “does not work for anyone carrying a sail, a kayak or a wing.” The ferry’s parking is solved on paper and paid for in restrictions across the south side of the waterfront.

The plan calls itself a Year 1 plan, to be adjusted to actual demand; adjustments could include “changes to parking fees, permit types and restrictions, and the location and extent of time and duration limits.”

Sources and figures
ObligationProtect the parking that sailing, swimming, paddling and board sports depend on.
ObstacleFerry riders need 314 to 347 all-day stalls on weekdays in the first year; the plan has 265.
The planSend all-day parkers to 265 paid stalls, or to free parking on Marina Blvd and University Ave.
Reality checkCommuters are projected to fill the paid stalls, and the free all-day parking is up to a third of a mile from the launches. The Draft EIR heard that ferry parking would crowd out swimmers, windsurfers, kayakers and anglers, and analyzed it as car noise.
Who bears itSailors, swimmers, paddlers, board sports, families at Shorebird Park
Can it be undone?Reversible by the City in principle; the plan exists because the ferry needs it.

The voyage · VII · Holding the risk

WETA can cut the service. Berkeley keeps the pier.

WETA’s access policy makes local jurisdictions own, maintain and fund terminal parking and landside assets. Its funding plan lists service cuts on underperforming routes as a way to stretch its money.

The plan
No enforceable service commitment or exit condition appears in the project record.
Reality check
Service can end by a board vote. A 50-year pier, a breakwater, a dredged channel and 40 removed trees do not revert, and there is no refund on the $100-million-plus if the ferry fails.
Why it matters

The division is written into WETA’s policy. Local jurisdictions “will retain or shall assume responsibility for managing, operating, maintaining, owning, rehabilitating, constructing, and funding terminal access programs and improvements.” WETA runs the boats.

When WETA’s money runs short, its plan names the lever: “service adjustments on underperforming routes.” The pier, the breakwater and the reorganized lots stay where they are. So does the obligation to maintain them.

Sources and figures
ObligationA service commitment as durable as the structures built for it.
ObstacleService is a WETA Board decision; the assets are Berkeley’s.
The planNo enforceable service commitment or exit condition appears in the project record.
Reality checkService can end by a board vote. A 50-year pier, a breakwater, a dredged channel and 40 removed trees do not revert, and there is no refund on the $100-million-plus if the ferry fails.
Who bears itBerkeley, as owner
Can it be undone?Service: reversible by WETA. Structures, dredging, tree removal: not reversible.

A cautionary tale

Richmond got its riders without remaking a park. It still costs about $36 a rider.

Richmond’s terminal cost about $20 million: a float, a gangway and a 362-space lot beside an old Ford plant. Berkeley’s is $103.6 million before boats, with a breakwater, $26 million of dredging, and a parking lot carved from a waterfront park.

The plan
The business plan’s cost model: about $13 a boarding in 2035, fare and subsidy together.
Reality check
By WETA’s budget figures, Richmond costs about $36.50 a rider to run, and the full fare is $4.70: fares cover roughly 13%. It has a county sales tax behind it. Berkeley has none, and its terminal costs about five times as much to build.
Why it matters

Richmond is WETA’s success story: the strongest weekday recovery in the system, 953 riders a day. It got there with a low fare, a modest terminal and a lot that was already paved. Its weekend service still struggles: 515 riders a day, “highly seasonable,” on a schedule WETA calls “not particularly robust.”

Its riders are regional. Of riders leaving Richmond for San Francisco, 55% start their trip in Richmond; the rest come from San Pablo, Albany, El Cerrito, El Sobrante, Kensington, and Berkeley, 9%. Of riders coming home, 60% end the trip in Richmond, and 8% go on to El Cerrito. Richmond’s riders are also the most likely in the system to switch from BART: 65% name BART or rail as their alternative.

Berkeley proposes the same kind of service at five times the construction cost, built by changing a park in ways that cannot be undone. If Berkeley’s ridership matches Richmond’s, the operating bill will look like Richmond’s, and Berkeley has no Measure J to pay it.

The $36.50 is an estimate of Richmond’s operating cost per rider, computed from WETA’s figures: $10,755,060 (FY2025 budget) over 953 weekday riders × 255 days plus 515 weekend riders × 100 days, the day counts WETA’s business plan uses. Riders are read as boardings, and the farebox figure uses the full $4.70 fare; discount fares would push it lower. Matching actual expenditure, boarding and fare-revenue totals for Richmond would replace the estimate. It is an estimate for Richmond, not a Berkeley forecast; the business plan’s Berkeley figure is about $13 a boarding in 2022 dollars. Richmond’s $20 million is the estimate at its groundbreaking, years before Berkeley’s 2025 estimate; inflation narrows the five-to-one gap but does not close it. Survey origins and destinations are trip ends, not home addresses; respondents who gave the same city for both were removed.

Sources and figures
ObligationA route that pays its way closer than Richmond’s does, or a named source for the difference.
ObstacleRichmond carries about as many weekday riders as Berkeley is projected to, after the biggest fare cut in the system: $7 to $4.50, now $4.70.
The planThe business plan’s cost model: about $13 a boarding in 2035, fare and subsidy together.
Reality checkBy WETA’s budget figures, Richmond costs about $36.50 a rider to run, and the full fare is $4.70: fares cover roughly 13%. It has a county sales tax behind it. Berkeley has none, and its terminal costs about five times as much to build.
Who bears itBerkeley, if its route performs like Richmond’s
Can it be undone?Richmond’s terminal changed little; Berkeley’s changes to the park do not revert.

In sum

A yes commits Berkeley to all of it

  • A remade shoreline: a 1,080-foot pier, a 400-foot breakwater and up to 400,000 cubic yards of dredging.
  • A reorganized waterfront: once the ferry runs, four-hour limits or permits on every lot near the sailing docks and the beach for anyone who arrives after 6 a.m.
  • A fleet promise with no fleet behind it: electric boats in the EIR, diesel in the business plan.
  • Half of an operating subsidy, as WETA’s Board expects: at least $4.5 million a year, with no plan to pay it, for a regional service. The City says Berkeley is not required to pay it.
  • The parking, access and landside assets, permanently, whatever WETA later decides about service.

Council votes November 17. Tell them before then.

On Tuesday, November 17, the City Council is scheduled to decide whether to certify the environmental review and approve the project. WETA is urging residents to press for a yes.

Ask Council to vote no until the plan answers what the record leaves open: who pays to run the boats after 2034, what Berkeley owes if WETA cuts service, and how the South Cove stays usable for the people who use it now.

  • Write. Email council@berkeleyca.gov. Letters received early reach every member in the supplemental packets the City compiles five days and one day before the meeting.
  • Speak. Public comment at the 6 p.m. meeting, in person or on Zoom. The agenda, posted at berkeleyca.gov/council-agendas, gives the location and the item number.
  • Put every issue on the record now. The City’s agenda notice says that in a lawsuit over a use permit, “the issues and evidence will be limited to those raised by you or someone else, orally or in writing, at a public hearing or prior to the close of the last public hearing on the project.”
